intro: The moment a model spans GPUs, part of every step is spent talking instead of computing. How much depends on which collective operations the parallelism strategy needs, how big each message is, and which link carries it. This lesson covers NCCL and its collectives, a simple latency-plus-bandwidth model for predicting communication time, why decode-time tensor parallelism is latency-bound while prefill is bandwidth-bound, how to measure links with nccl-tests, and the settings that most often break multi-node jobs.
objectives: Name the NCCL collectives and which parallelism strategy uses each
Estimate communication time with a latency plus size-over-bandwidth model
Explain why small decode messages make TP latency-bound
Benchmark GPU links with nccl-tests and read algorithm versus bus bandwidth
Diagnose common multi-node networking failures from NCCL logs

blocks.text: **NCCL** (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) is what inference engines and training frameworks call to move data between GPUs. It discovers the topology (NVLink, NVSwitch, PCIe, InfiniBand, RoCE), picks algorithms such as **ring** or **tree**, and runs the transfers as GPU kernels, which is why they appear on Nsight timelines. AMD's equivalent is RCCL.

rows: Every GPU ends with the sum of everyone's data
Every GPU ends with everyone's pieces concatenated
Sum, then each GPU keeps one slice
Each GPU sends a different chunk to every other

blocks.text: A useful first model: time = **alpha** + size / **bandwidth**. Alpha is a fixed latency per operation (launch, synchronisation, link latency); the second term is the transfer. Large messages are dominated by bandwidth, small ones by alpha. A ring all-reduce across N GPUs moves about 2 x (N-1)/N times the message size through each GPU, which is why nccl-tests reports **bus bandwidth** (busbw), corrected for that factor, alongside raw algorithm bandwidth.

blocks.caption: Decode-step TP traffic (illustrative model and timings)
blocks.code:
hidden size 8192, batch 32, FP16 activations:
  message = 32 x 8192 x 2 bytes = 512 KiB per all-reduce
80 layers x 2 all-reduces = 160 all-reduces per decode step

if each takes ~20 us on NVLink  -> ~3.2 ms per step
if each takes ~100 us on a slower path -> ~16 ms per step
(compare a decode step of ~20-30 ms: the slow path eats most of it)

blocks.text: Decode messages are small and frequent, so tensor parallelism at decode time is **latency-bound**: what matters is how fast each tiny all-reduce completes, which NVLink and NVSwitch do in microseconds and network links cannot match. Prefill messages are large (thousands of tokens), so prefill is **bandwidth-bound**. Engines and libraries fight the latency term with fused communication kernels and by overlapping communication with computation.

Before trusting a multi-GPU deployment, measure the fabric. NVIDIA's `nccl-tests` sweep message sizes and report latency and bandwidth per collective. Run them on every new node type and after any driver, firmware or network change.

blocks.caption: Single node, 8 GPUs, then 8 nodes over the network
blocks.code:
# all-reduce from 8 bytes to 1 GiB, doubling each step, on 8 local GPUs
./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 1G -f 2 -g 8

# multi-node with MPI: 64 ranks, 8 per node, one GPU per rank
mpirun -np 64 -N 8 ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 8G -f 2 -g 1

items: Look at **small-message latency** (top rows) for decode-time TP and **large-message busbw** (bottom rows) for prefill and KV transfer.
Compare busbw with the link's rated bandwidth; a large shortfall points at topology, configuration or a faulty link.
Inside a node, numbers should reflect NVLink; if they look like PCIe, the GPUs are not using NVLink.

sections.heading: Designing to keep communication off the critical path

blocks.text: Communication cost is not fixed; architecture choices move it. Keep the most frequent, latency-sensitive collectives on the fastest links: tensor parallelism inside an NVLink domain, never across a datacenter network. Send the less frequent, larger transfers, pipeline activations and KV-cache handoffs, over the inter-node fabric, where bandwidth matters more than latency.

Batch size also changes the picture. Larger decode batches make each all-reduce message bigger but amortise the fixed latency over more tokens, so communication per token falls. Overlap helps too: modern engines start sending one layer's results while computing the next, hiding part of the cost. When you see NCCL kernels taking a large share of a profiled step, the usual fixes, in order, are a smaller TP size with more replicas, keeping TP within NVLink, and only then faster or more network links.

For expert parallelism the all-to-all exchange is both large and frequent, and uneven expert popularity makes some GPUs wait for others. Rack-scale NVLink domains, careful expert placement and load balancing exist largely to tame this. If you serve large mixture-of-experts models, budget as much engineering time for the network as for the GPUs.
Set `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` and read the start-up lines: NCCL prints which transports it chose for each GPU pair (P2P over NVLink, SHM, NET over IB or Socket). Most failures are visible there.

rows: Transport shows NET/Socket instead of IB
RDMA devices not visible or not selected
Expose IB devices to the container; set NCCL_IB_HCA
Wrong network interface or blocked ports
Set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the right interface; open ports
PCIe topology, GPUDirect RDMA off, MTU
Check nvidia-smi topo -m, enable GPUDirect, fix MTU
Check NVLink and NIC error counters; look at fabric congestion

blocks.text: In containers and Kubernetes, multi-node GPU jobs typically need host networking or an RDMA-capable network plugin, the InfiniBand devices mounted, and enough locked memory. Validate with nccl-tests inside the same pod spec you will use for serving.

practice.title: Measure your fabric before you trust it
steps: On a multi-GPU instance, build nccl-tests and run all_reduce_perf across all local GPUs from 8 bytes to 1 GiB.
Record latency at 8 KiB to 1 MiB and busbw at 256 MiB and above.
Run `nvidia-smi topo -m` and relate the numbers to the links shown.
Restrict the test to two GPUs connected over PCIe (if any) and compare small-message latency.
Using the decode traffic model above, estimate communication time per step for a model you care about at TP 2, 4 and 8.
Write down the TP size beyond which communication would exceed 20% of a 25 ms step on your fabric.

focus: NCCL picks transports and algorithms; collectives run as GPU kernels.
TP uses all-reduce; EP uses all-to-all; PP and KV transfer use send/recv.
Time ~ alpha + size / bandwidth: small messages are latency-bound.
Decode TP is latency-bound, so it needs NVLink-class links.
Measure with nccl-tests: latency for small sizes, busbw for large.
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows which transport was chosen.

pitfalls: Deploying TP across nodes without measuring small-message latency.
Containers that cannot see the InfiniBand devices, silently falling back to TCP sockets.
Reading algorithm bandwidth as if it were link bandwidth.
Skipping nccl-tests after driver, firmware or network changes.

quiz.q: Which collective does tensor parallelism rely on in every transformer layer?
quiz.explain: Each GPU computes a partial result for its slice of the layer, and an all-reduce sums those partials so every GPU has the full output.

quiz.q: Why is decode-time tensor parallelism usually latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound?
options: Its all-reduce messages are small and frequent, so fixed per-operation latency dominates
Decode runs on the CPU while prefill runs on the GPU
quiz.explain: A decode step all-reduces activations for the current batch only, hundreds of kilobytes, many times per step. With small messages the alpha term outweighs size over bandwidth.

quiz.q: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows NET/Socket for traffic between nodes that have InfiniBand adapters. What is the likely problem?
options: The RDMA devices are not visible or not selected, so NCCL fell back to TCP
The GPUs are connected by NVLink
The model is too large for the cluster
quiz.explain: When NCCL cannot use the IB devices, often because the container cannot see them, it falls back to sockets over Ethernet, which is much slower.

quiz.q: In nccl-tests output, what does the busbw column help you judge?
options: How close the collective gets to the hardware link bandwidth
The latency of a single 8-byte message
How many requests per second the model can serve
quiz.explain: Bus bandwidth corrects algorithm bandwidth for how much data the collective actually moves, so it can be compared with the rated bandwidth of the links.

quiz.q: Each decode step does 160 all-reduces at about 100 microseconds each on a slow path. Roughly how much time per step is communication?
quiz.explain: 160 x 100 microseconds = 16,000 microseconds = 16 ms, which would consume most of a typical decode step.
